what_its_for: Methscopolamine is used to treat stomach ulcers and to help reduce stomach acid, cramps, and spasms in your digestive tract. It works by slowing down the activity of your stomach and intestines, which helps relieve pain and discomfort.
how_to_take: Take this medicine by mouth, usually 30 minutes before meals and at bedtime, or exactly as your doctor tells you. Swallow the tablet whole with a full glass of water. You can take it with or without food, but taking it before meals usually works best. Do not crush or chew the tablet unless your doctor says it is okay.
dosing: The usual adult dose is 2.5 mg taken 30 minutes before each meal and 2.5 to 5 mg at bedtime. Your doctor may adjust your dose based on how well it works for you and any side effects you have. Never take more than your doctor prescribed. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next scheduled dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do not take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one, as this can increase your risk of side effects.
storage: Store this medicine at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C and 25°C). Keep it away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Do not use the medicine after the expiration date printed on the label.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking this medicine, as it can increase drowsiness and dizziness. Avoid driving, operating heavy machinery, or doing anything that requires clear vision or sharp mental alertness until you know how this medicine affects you. Avoid getting overheated or becoming dehydrated, especially in hot weather or during exercise, because this medicine reduces your ability to sweat. Avoid taking antacids at the same time as this medicine — take antacids at least 1 hour after taking methscopolamine.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away if you experience: difficulty urinating or no urination at all, severe constipation or bloating, fast or irregular heartbeat, eye pain or vision changes (such as blurred vision or seeing halos around lights), high fever combined with hot dry skin and confusion, signs of a serious allergic reaction such as rash, swelling of the face or throat, or trouble breathing. Also call your doctor if your stomach symptoms are not improving or are getting worse.
when_it_works: You may start to feel some relief from stomach cramps and discomfort within 30 to 60 minutes of taking your first dose. For the full benefit in treating ulcers and reducing stomach acid problems, it may take several days to a few weeks of regular use. Continue taking it as prescribed even if you start feeling better.
special_populations: Older adults (65 years and older) should use this medicine with extra caution because they are more sensitive to its side effects, especially confusion, dizziness, difficulty urinating, and constipation. This medicine is generally not recommended during pregnancy unless clearly needed — talk to your doctor about the risks and benefits. It is not known if this medicine passes into breast milk, so breastfeeding mothers should consult their doctor before use. This medicine is not approved for use in children. If you have glaucoma, an enlarged prostate, urinary problems, heart disease, liver disease, kidney disease, or bowel blockage, tell your doctor before taking this medicine, as it may not be safe for you.
